¶1 Auzubillah Minashaitan Nirajeem

¶2 Bismillah-ir-Rahman-ir-Rahim

¶3 If you remember last week we said that there are different dispositions of the Sufi. In some Sufi fear is overwhelming, in some of them love is overwhelming, in some of them renunciation of duniya is powerful and in some of them they are after maarifah, knowledge about God rather than anything else. So these are different inclinations in Sufism. Now, mysticism of fear we discussed about Hassan al Basri. We have one other person, who we did not discuss, that's Al Haris al Muhasibi who is a very important figure. I don't know whether we discussed him or not. I don't think so. This figure is important because he influenced later mysticism, especially his influence on Ghazali was very overwhelming and you will see Ghazali in his book Al Harith al Muhasibi very frequently and he lived about 3 centuries before Ghazali.

¶4 However his influence was there. He was born in Basra in 781 AH. He was probably influenced by the teachings of Hassan Al Basri, his follower since he was born in Basra and you remember we said Hassan Basri was. A Mystic whose fear was very overwhelming, and then his name was derived from Muhasabha, the constant analysis of even the most secret motions of the soul and the heart, and this is a concept which is still persistent in our mysticism to do muhasabha ie count to calculate ones action, even feelings, even attitudes every night or every week or during the life frequently do it. So since he was doing this very much, he was stressing on this concept of Mahasabha, calculation of the action.

¶5 So he was Muhasibi. He taught the relentless fight against man's lower nature, not just the odd struggle of the ascetic against the flesh but the subtle psychological analysis of what we thought that the concept of Mahasabha, which is usually, mentioned in nowadays Irfan. And he wrote books on mystical psychology, one of the earlier writers of mystical concept was this Al Haris al Muhasibi. As I said, he included Ghazali because his writings were extent at that time and Ghazali used to read Muhasib’s writings. Muhasib’s subtle analysis of riyaa and his whole methodological approach became fundamental and indispensable to the early Sufis and also to later Sufis. Then his influence became very apparent on a group of Sufis who were called Malamatiyah, people of blame.

¶6 Now he was stressing that whatever you do should not be mixed with riyaa with ostentation, showing off. Now this if we take it to extreme, it means that you should not want people to admire you for what you do. Now of course, as you have in the Quran, they did not observe the content that they should. Have so we have Sufis who actually they did things to bring blames upon themselves. For example, they're very pious people, but they drank wine in front of the people. And maybe they didn't drink it. Or they just hold as drinking wine while they were drinking water, but they did it so that people tell them that they drink wine, they are fasiq, fajir, kafir.

¶7 They didn't want to actually care about what people were saying about them and this let some Sufis to do very abhorrent things in front of the people. And this was one of the reasons that at times there were detestation. They were despised for Sufi, saying that they do lots of horrible things in front of people they do not care about Sharia. They do not care about anything related to religion. However, the root of it for some of them, for some of them, was this stress on the concept that you should not have ostentation or riyaa. Of course then later Sufis came and somehow corrected it. They said, when we say you shouldn't have riyaa, that you shouldn't care about what people say about you, whether good or bad.

¶8 Now you don't want people say good things about you, but you do bad things and you want people to say bad things about you. This is again doing things because of the people and in fact it's very interesting how Shaitan sometimes deceive people because some of these Sufis, they did these blame worthy things to show off to other sufis and look how we do this, blame worthy things so that people blame us and we do not want to do riyaa. Whatever you do, Shaitan finds a way to these things in one way or another. It is he who gave Sufism highly developed technical language. Many of these concepts that we use in today’s mysticism are developed in the 2^(nd) and 3^(rd) century starting with muhasabha and even before him and Ghazali, the Master of Moderate medieval mysticism depends largely upon him as I mentioned on Muhasibi.

¶9 Now then we come to mysticism of zuhd or renunciation and we have very though mystics for renunciation. When we say we have fear or renunciation of love, we don't mean that these people exclusively had renunciation or love or fear or whatever. It means that they gave more preference to this concept rather than others. We have sufis who were not zahid at all. They did not renounce it; they did not take themselves away from worldly benefits or pleasures. However, they were zahid in their hearts and we have other Sufis like these people whom we see Ibrahim bin Adham who died 162 hijra. He was a contemporary of Imam Sadiq (as) and Imam Kazim (as), Fuzail bin Ayaz and Shaqeeq Balkhi.

¶10 All of them were related somehow to our immah and especially Shaqeeq Balkhi we will discuss the book Ismaul Shayaat Imam Sadiq (as). Some people say that it was written by Shaqeeq Balkhi and it was attributed to Imam Jafar Sadiq (as). We'll come to that later. Now let's go to Ibrahim Adham. I think we touched on Ibrahim Adham last week a little bit. He was the Prince in Balkh and of course all these ascetics came from Khorasan, the land of asceticism. He, of course, born and grown in Balkh and Junaid used to call him the key of mystical sciences. Junaid of Baghdad who lived in the 4^(th) century was the turn a turning point in old mystical knowledge because many of the mystical knowledge that we have now goes back to Junaid.

¶11 He somehow was the architect of this kind of mystical understanding and mystical jargan and language. All mystics whether Shia or Sunni pledge tribute to Junaid of Baghdad. He calls Abrahim Adham the key of mystical sciences because he somehow theorized these sciences of mysticism in the way we spoke. He learned from Imam Sadiq (as) while he was still very young and he renounced the princely life in Balkh and became in Islamic tradition, one of the proverbial examples of poverty, absence and trust in god since he just left his palace while he was a prince without any provision just seeking the pleasure of god. So he’s proverbial. He is like Buddha. Usually they correspond between Abrahim Adham and Buddha.

¶12 They say they very similar lines coming from princely background and then going to desert or to jungle and then starting to preach people, illuminations coming to their hearts and he is credited with making the first classification of the stage of zuhd. Now this is where, of course he died in 162 hijra. You will see how well he was theorizing about these issues of zuhd and other mystical concepts. He says that renunciation has 3 levels. First is renunciation of the world. This is zuhd that you have to renounce whatever pleasure you can see in this world. And then renunciation of the happy feeling of having achieved renunciation because when you become zahid you say Alhamdulillah, I don't love anything in this world.

¶13 Now this happiness should go away. Some of these mystics are very difficult to analyse how they thought about their relationship with God. They wanted complete, complete attention to the Lord. And since of course in his time and later on many imposters they started to talk about zuhd and other issues. These real Sufis they try to say that if you are real zahid you shouldn't be happy about your zuhd because this is again something which diverts you from God and we have one saying of Amirul momineen about zuhd in Nahjul Balagha, saying that the best of zuhd or renunciation is to conceal your zuhd. Now how can you conceal your zuhd? By looking very lavishly, having a very lavish type of life but not actually having them.

¶14 There is one early mystic even earlier than Ibrahim, Sufiyan Thawri. He was a contemporary of Imam Jafar Sadiq (as) and once he saw Imam Jafar having a very precious a very luxurious, kingly dress. He had put on and he had attended a meeting. And he went and said, is this is going with your type of thinking about religion and God? Then Imam just took that away that dress and showed a dress beneath it, which was a very harsh which was actually quite uncomfortable to wear and he said, this is how you have to be. You shouldn't show off your zuhd. The best type of zuhd is that you cover that you are a zahid. And here of course, these are the concepts taken from immah coming from that direction and the stage in which the 3rd stage of course in which the world is regarded as so unimportant that they did not talk about having zuhd of duniya at all.

¶15 You remember this call of Imam Ali (as) which is repeated several times in Nahjul Balagha that this world of you or this ruler ship of you is given less than the bone of a pig which is in hands of a leopard. You cannot talk about zuhd here. The bone of a pig is in hands of a sick man. You never want to go and take it. You say I want to turn away from it, I have to have zuhd. I have to renounce it. You renounce something which is valuable, isn't it? When you have zuhd, it means that the world is valuable and you want to turn away from it. Now if the world for you becomes like that bone of the pig in the hand of a sick man, would you talk about renouncing it at?

¶16 That’s out of place anymore. Now this is of course much higher than the previous one having zuhd towards duniya are and then not being happy for that zuhd. The 3rd is that you don't care at all about what happens in this world. It is less than what should go into your attention. It doesn't catch your attention at all. So of course this is a nice type of classification in the 2^(nd) century of how mystics should have zuhd or renunciation and in another hades he is reported to have said, zuhd is of 3 types. 1^(st) is the compulsive zuhd, 2^(nd) is meritorious zuhd. It is veritable. It's not compulsory, but it's veritable. And the 3^(rd) is renunciation which brings you safety.

¶17 So its renunciation of safety. Now, what are these? The compulsive zuhd is to have zuhd towards what is haram. This is compulsive or to turn away from what is haram. So this is one type of zuhd. The veritable zuhd is to turn away from even what is halal for the sake of, of course something higher and above. And the zuhd of safety is to turn away from what is ambiguous. You don't know something, whether it's halal or not. You seek taqwa, the taqwa says yes; some people say yes, it's OK. Some people say no. But when you want to do it, there is something in the heart. Well, if you want to be safe just turn away from it.

¶18 Just. And this is another type of zuhd. So these types of classifications coming in the 2^(nd) century AH, of course they are valuable. He was the reporter as well. Reporters had this hades from prophet and Imam Sadiq (as) and from Sufiyan Thawri and from Malik ibne Dinar and others. And a person called Muhammad ibne Ishaq ibne Yahya who died 395 AH, towards the end of the 4^(th) century, has written a book called Musnad-e- Ibrahim Adham. When they write in musnad of someone it means all the hades that they have reported from the prophet through a chain. So it means that he reported a considerable amount of hades from the prophet. So he was Mohaddes Ibrahim Adham.

¶19 However it’s a very small book. It's only 49 pages. We come to a more mythical personality of mysticism of renunciation that's prevailed in Fudayl ibne Iyad. His story is more interesting than Ibrahim Adham. Now I tell you why. He died 187 so he wore contemporary to Imam Kazim & Imam Reza (as) and he has actually lots of stories from these immah. He was born in Samarkand in Khurasan, lived in Kufa and died in Mecca. So when you want to call him you say Fudayl ibne Iyad Samarqandi or Kufi or Makki. You bring all these kitties just lined them up one after another. He is known for his great fear and abundant crying and he was in his early life, a highwayman but later repented upon hearing the verse from Surah Al Hadid when he had climbed a wall to find access to his beloved girl.

¶20 It's very interesting. He actually climbed the wall and someone was reciting Quran in the house. He was a young man and the verse was “Alam ya'ni lil lazeena aamanooo an takhsha'a quloobuhum lizikril laahi wa maa nazala minal haqq” 57:16 isn't it the time for the believer that their hearts become humble towards Allah and upon hearing this he said yes, it is time, my Lord. And he just went back and went to the desert and started a very, very austere life to repent of what he had done in the highwayman and climbing walls of people. It is said in the story that in the Quran it is mentioned Alam ya'ni lil lazeena aamanooo, it is not the time.

¶21 He said, yes the time has come and he repented and it was a tawba tun nasooh of course and he became a very great personality in mysticism, actually reported abundantly from Imam Sadiq (as) again. Now, Al-Waheed al-Behbahani is the figure head of the usuli movement in Shia jurisprudence. Of course, he is a very knowledgeable personality. He regards himself to be a Shia due to a hades that he reports from Imam Sadiq (as) blaming some Sunni ulema which is reported in Al-Kafi. It's interesting, Kafi as well reports the hades of Fudayl ibne Iyad and you could see that the high hierarchy could become a reporter whose hades are now in the most authentic books of both Shia and Sunni.

¶22 He is a reliable reporter in both the Shia and Sunni world, as Zahabi mentions that there is consensus among all scholars regarding his reliability and his dignity and names him as Shaikhul Islam and both Kulaini and Bukhari report this hades in Al-Kafi and this is very interesting that he is reliable both for the Shia and the Sunni ulema. He appeared in these 2 very authentic books of the 2 sects. Scholars such as Sufiyan Thawri, Sufyan ibn Uyaynah and As-Shafi reports hades from him and his school in Mecca is now visited by scholars. I don't know where it is. Next time, when I go I would like to find out where the tomb of Fudayl ibne Iyad is situated in Mecca.

¶23 And about him Al-Qushayri writes in his risalah, of course, Al-Qushayri is a mystic of the 4^(th) and 5^(th) century, a very prominent one and the one who has theorized the many mystical concepts. He said and when he died, sadness was taken away from the world, meaning that his heart was so fearful and so sad. When he was praying and thinking about God, that when he died, when he passed away, sadness was taken. Of course, this is exaggeration. He said a very nice phrase about someone if he wanted to praise him. Now we come to another personality, Shaqiq ibne Ibrahim al-Balkhi. He is again from Khorasan in Balkh. He was killed in battlefield in Gilan in north Iran.

¶24 And he had several stories as well and mystic of austere, zuhd and asceticism. He's usually mentioned as an exemplar of asceticism and he has reported many hades from Ahlul Bait and from people whom he did not name because it was abandoned in his town to name people reporting from Ahlul Bait. And he also reports from Ibrahim Al Adham whom we discussed previously and Sufiyan Thawri. Many people have reported hades from him, among them Hatem ul Aasem, nicknamed as Luqman of this ummah. Of course we do not discuss Hatem ul Aasem though he is a very great mystic but we are just handpicking a few mystics from 2^(nd) and 3^(rd) century to discuss because if you want to discuss all these mystics it would need really several sessions.

¶25 Hatem means deaf. You know, he was not deaf. But he had a story. Once a lady went to him and asked him a question and inadvertently the lady released some wind with sound. And she became very embarrassed and he felt that embarrassment. And he said, what did you say? I didn't hear. And the lady spoke louder. And he again said, what did you say? I didn't hear and the lady made sure that this person is deaf. And she became relieved of her embarrassment. And that's why later on; he was called Hatem ul Aasem. It is actually praise for his personality, the way he treated just an ordinary lady coming to him. So he also reports from from Shaqiq.

¶26 And his classification of the scholars of religion is famous and his story with Imam Kazim (as) is famous as well. His classification about the scholars of religion, this is in Munyatul Mureed of Shahid al-Thani. Actually Shia scholars very much rely on sayings of Shaqiq Balkhi although well the Sunni’s regarded him to be Sunni, it’s interesting that the mystics usually do not reveal very much about their mazhab. They were very free of this and. No one even knew what type of mazhab they were following. Of course not all of them but some of them were like this. Now he said that the scholars are of 3 types. First is someone who knows God but doesn't know the command of God, doesn't know Sharia, but he knows god.

¶27 He is a mystic but doesn't know jurisprudence. Second is a servant on whose heart the divine knowledge has illuminated and he emerged in the vision of the Jalal and Kibriya of the lord. He doesn't know anything about jurisprudence. He hasn't gone into studying that. And third is someone who knows the commands of God but doesn't know God. This is a criticism of Jews as well that they know the command of God, what is right; what is wrong, what is halal, what is haram. But they don't know what is God. This is the person who knows halal and haram and the minute details of ahkam, they know. But they don't know the secrets of the glory of god.

¶28 The third type is those who know God and know the commands of God. And then he says these are the people who are sitting on a borderline between this world and the next world. When they return to god they don't know anything about this world. When they turn to this world they are like ordinary people. They talk to them, they teach them and then he says this is the meaning of hades from the prophet who said, “Ask from the scholars (ulema), mix with the wise people (huqamah) and sit with the great”. Then he said who the ulema and huqamah are? Who are the great people? The prophet means those who know the command of God, but you know do not know God well.

¶29 Certainly you never go to a mystic and ask them about a fatwa on moon sighting for example, they don't know. And if you do go, you have gone to the wrong place. Therefore the prophet said, ask the scholars of jurisprudence if you have a question. However, this is not enough, of course. Just knowing what is halal and what is haram is not enough. You act upon it, but this doesn't give life to your heart. Therefore, the prophet said apart from this mix with the wise people with the mystics but restrict them with those who know God, who are close to God. However the most important thing is sit with the great people who know both jurisprudence and who have the knowledge of God.

¶30 Now, of course it wasn't very important that's why I did not translate it. Actually, just wanted to very quickly touch upon it. Now the story he has with Imam Kazim (as). I just mentioned a summary of this story. This is a very nice story. Has anyone already heard this story of Shaqiq al Balkhi with Imam Kazim (as)? At the time of Shaqiq there were many pretenders of Sufism who pretended that there were Sufis and they actually put the burden of their life upon other people. It was a means of living for some people, they pretended that they were Sufis and people provided them with their services. Now he says that. This is of course reported by Ibn Jawzi who's a Sunni scholar.

¶31 He says that in year 149, he said at a test. Now this is the first year of Imam Kazim (as) because Imam Sadiq(as) died in the year 148. He says in 149, I was going to hajj and I at the manzil of qadisiyah, you know there were manazel. There were resting places. In resting place when I settled down, I saw a very, very handsome young gentleman. He was white colour not white, of course. And he had worn a woollen cloth like the Sufis. He didn't have proper shoes and he was sitting aloof from other people. I said, well, he was a big mystic himself. I said, this is one of these young people who want to put the burden on this caravan so that everyone goes and serves them.

¶32 And I said to myself, wallah I will go and rebuke this young man that you shouldn't do this. You should come like other people, take off this dress and come to hajj like other people. As soon as I neared him and he saw me. He said “Ya Shaqiq, keep away from lots of suspicions because some suspicions are seen. I was suddenly shocked. What did this young man said to me? I was thinking about him and he said such a thing. I said in my heart, No! This is not the person I thought. He is a nice. He spoke about what is in my heart. I will go and I will follow him to see what type of person he is.

¶33 However, as soon as I wanted to go to join him, he disappeared. I didn't see. I couldn't see, so I lost. I lost him until another manzil which was called Muwaqisa. Suddenly I saw that this young man was standing praying and all his body was shaking and the tears was coming down from his eyes. I said I will go and apologize him because of what I thought. When I went there he quickly finished his salah and recited a verse of the Quran. “Wa innee la Ghaffaarul liman taaba wa aamana wa 'amila saalihan summah tadaa” 20:82 He didn't speak, but from the Quran and he said this verse that Allah says I am forgiving for whoever repents and do good, and then they find the way.

¶34 I said Abdaal, Abdaal is a group of Sufis who the Sufis think that are one of those for whom God actually provides for everyone in in this earth. I said, this is one of them. Twice he mentioned what is in my heart but I couldn't follow him. He was very elusive. I couldn't actually catch up with him. We went to another manzil. I found that he had a jug. He was trying to put it down into a well, bringing water up and suddenly the jug fell from his hand. And he said he looked towards the sky and said “My lord, You are the one who provides me with water when I'm thirsty and the one who provide me with food when I'm hungry and you know that I didn't have anything but that jug.

¶35 The junk fell into the well”. Shaqiq said I swear by God, I saw the water of the well coming up and bringing the jug with itself up to reaching his hand and he took some water with the jug and went and made wudhu. And many other stories, of course, it's long. He said, again I asked him. He couldn't actually spot Imam in this because he wanted to be alone and he was alone for himself. He said until when I went to Kaaba to do tawaaf, I saw him there. He was beside Kaaba. Until we went to Mecca, I saw him standing by the gutter of the House. In the middle of the night, very humbly crying, beseeching and praying.

¶36 And I wanted to talk to him but he did not stop crying and praying until morning. And when the fajr came, he sat on his musallah on his sajadah started to say tasbeeh. Then he did his Salahtul fajr. When he went, did a tawaaf and then he got out of the house, and I followed him to see where he goes. While I said this man is someone which you cannot find on the earth. And when he went out, I saw that he went to a big house where there were lots of relatives, lots of slaves, people, money, property, everything. Suddenly he became a very, very rich and respectable person. This was not the man I had seen on the way when we were coming from Mecca, and people had surrounded him and they were taking blessing from him.

¶37 I went to one of those people and asked who this man is? That man replied that he is Musa ibne Jafar. I said I would have been surprised if these amazing things would have come from someone but a person like Musa ibne Jafar. So this is a very famous story that he Shaqiq reports from Imam Kazim (as) and you will see how the Mystic actually separated themselves in level from people like immah. They were completely different, completely different in terms of their calibre of understanding and how they behave.

¶38 Now we go to mysticism of love. So we covered mysticism of fear and mysticism of renunciation, mysticism of love, definition of love by Imam Sadiq (as) which was repeated by later mystics, love is a divine fire that devolves man completely. Now this this has been taken by many mystics and I think if you go to any book of mysticism speaking about God, they repeat this sentence, which is reported from Imam Sadiq (as). We have 3 figures here which were overwhelmingly showing love rather than fear or ascetic life. Of course they were different at different stages, but eventually they became very famous in this aspect of love. We have Maruf al-Karkhi who was from Iraq and died at the end of the 2nd century.

¶39 Rabaa Al-Adawiya who was again from Basra, Iraq and Dhul-Nun al-Misri from Egypt. Now Maruf al-Karkhi of course, spoke about divine love. He was among the first to speak about divine love. He told that one cannot learn love for it is divine gift and not an acquisition. You can never acquire god’s love. It is given to you. His student, Sari al-Saqati was the first to discuss the various mystical states, Ahwaal and of course Saqati is very important, but he was a student of Maruf al-Karkhi. Now I want ask you a question and that is before going to the next mystic of love, how do you think this love is put in the heart of people? I mean, we know that you cannot acquire it, you cannot go and read the book and fall in love with God for example.

¶40 It's something which is put in your heart. How is it putting in your heart? It's of course you can say it's like knowledge which Allah puts in the heart to whomever he wants. However, there is something else in this. It is very important. God shows the face of himself to people which completely infatuates them and takes them out of their mind. They cannot think about anything else anymore. It’s not the love put to them but the face of Allah is shown to them, which is very lovely. And that's why they cannot think about anything else. And the love comes. That stage of our life not shown to everyone. It is only shown to those who deserve it.

¶41 And when they see it they cannot think about anything else. It's something which completely absorbed. It's just like when very, very of course, very simple and probably elusive example. But when 2 people fall in love with each other them probably like each other’s appearance and faith or they like each other’s behaviour or whatever. They see something as they fall in love. If you see something from god which is very beautiful to your heart, if God shows that face of himself then, of course, you fall in love with Allah and this cannot be removed by anyone. And that's why our immah always asked for this. Show us the faith of you that would absorb us in your love and that love, of course, would become completely different from the world you love, from the physical love.

¶42 It's something which should be experienced rather than should be talked about. And these people who talk about divine love they are not mad people or you can't say that they are taking these verses into their extreme thinking. No, Allah has shown them a face of himself which has completely absorbed them. And when we come to the story of Rabaa Al-Adawiya, you would see that he was she was certainly one of those who was absorbed completely and of course it depends on the capacity of the people. Sometimes you are absorbed in a way that you cannot talk about anything else. Sometimes the capacity is very high, like the prophets. Although the best face of Allah was shown to him, still he could live like other people.

¶43 And these mystics, of course, their capacities were limited and seeing that face of God had completely absorbed and annihilated them in thinking about nothing but Allah. When we come to Rabia you will see this. Rabaa Al-Adawiya, she was born to a very poor family. First of all, let me say something about Islam as mysticism and women, because our mystics have talked a lot about women and we have many women mystics actually. There was one woman mystic.

¶44 Q1. Not Audible

¶45 Ans: I don’t know which lady you are talking about. Maybe you're talking about Lady Amin, who just recently passed away. She was both a mystic and an interpreter of the Quran and a jurist. She was a mujtahidah. She passed away, I think 5-6 years ago. This of course belongs to the 2^(nd) century after Hijra.

¶46 Now Qaysari was a student of Ibe Arabi. He says in his commentary on Fusus al-Hikam that you should know that female observed in her reality is identical with men. What does he mean by observed in her reality? Means you divest them of the sex, male or female. In the reality of their being in the soul and the capabilities of the soul they are just like male. They could only be distinguished from each other when observed with their special features. When you look at them, the physical constitution you say this is male, this is female. Otherwise, when you look into the soul, there's no difference. Of course, I don't know. I'm not sure about this, the identical nature of male and female because I think they are even in the soul they are different and think differently.

¶47 And they can observe things differently. And this is the beauty of the creation. Allah has bestowed upon his male and female type of creation. Now, then he says the title of Saints was bestowed upon women equally with men. As opposed to Christianity, which very recently has happened, right from the beginning of mystical history in Islam, ladies were called AwliyaAllah as gentlemen were called AwliyaAllah as well. And since Islam has no order of priesthood and no priestly caste, there was nothing to prevent a woman from reaching the highest religious rank in the hierarchy of Muslim Saints. And that's true. Now with regards to Rabaa, she was woman of Al-Qays tribe. This is going back to tribe of al-Qaysīyya and since she was born in Basra, she was also known as Al Basaria, Rabia Al Basri.

¶48 When anyone speaking about mysticism of love, the first person who is discussed of course is not men. It is Rabia who was completely absorbed, probably because of her female nature as well. That love of God, the faith of God which actually gives love to the heart, had made her completely aloof from everything else. She was born probably about 95 or 99 AH in the poorest of homes. According to Attar, who wrote Tazkirat al-Awliya in Basra where she spent the greater part of her life and her father already had 3 daughters and so she was called Rabia, the fourth. So usually Rabia is not given as a name to the first or second or third born daughter.

¶49 However now after this Rabia, even the first born girls are called Rabia as well but Rabia means the fourth and that's why she was called Rabia. We can find material on here only in the memoir of the Saints of Attar in Tazkirat al-Awliya who lived more than 400 years after Rabia. The much of what he tells of her must be regarded as purely legendary because there are things mentioned about her which are impossible to have happened. However, mystics have made a myth of Rabia as the greatest woman mystic in the early mystical history. She's an Islamic saint and she's believed to have lived from 717 to 801 AH in what is now Iraq, while the poor orphan she was captured by a slave trader who proceeded to sell her into slavery.

¶50 As a slave, she was kept busy with her household duties until night but one night time released from her chores; she devoted herself to prayer, going without sleep to do so. One night her master caught sight of her absorbed in prayer. He was astonished to see a light miraculously appear over her head which illuminated the entire house. Now it's interesting because we have hades about Fatima Zahra (sa) which said why she was called Zahra, the shining and one of the reasons mentioned by immah is that when she stood to pray a light was emanating from her and illuminating the whole house and even the neighbourhood. And of course this is taken to be an exaggeration of the Shia.

¶51 However, you would see ordinary lady like Rabia, what the mystic would report about someone like Rabia it's quite similar. Going back to the story, the master was terrified. He went back to his room, where he sat in wonder till daybreak. At dawn he approached Rabia, told her what he had seen and gave her freedom. So she became a free slave woman and when she became renowned, of course, she received numerous offers of marriage which of course she declined and she did not marry. As an early mystic emerging Basra, Hermeticism are common features with that of Basra mystics, namely the austere asceticism known from Hassanul Basri. This was the beginning of course of her proceeding towards the final destination of this irfan.

¶52 During an illness, a friend asked her if she desired anything. How can you ask me such a question as what do I desire? She said, I swear by the glory of God that for 12 years I have desired fresh dates and I have not yet tested tasted them. I am a servant of God and what has a servant to do with desires. Now this is austere asceticism, meaning not eating dates for 12 years, although she desired to eat it. This is austere asceticism. I don't know whether this is a legend or not about but she moved from this later on, from this austere asceticism to mysticism of love. And it was her custom to pray all night, to sleep briefly just before dawn and then rise again just as dawn tinged the sky with gold.

¶53 Well, is a very poetical language of Attar mentioning the story of Rabia. However, her mystical path became quite distinguished from early Basra school, which was renowned for her fearful attitude. She taught that repentance was a gift from God. Now this is the starting point of her change in her mystical attitude from asceticism of fear. Now she talks about repentance and Allah, accepting her service with kindness. It was a gift from God because no one could repent unless God had already accepted him and given him this gift of repentance. She taught that sinners must fear the punishment they deserve for their sins. For some power she had held to a higher ideal worshipping God, neither from fear of hell nor for hope of paradise.

¶54 And completely devoting herself with god himself for she saw such self-interest as unworthy of God 's servants, emotions like fear and hope were like veils. Now this is going to vary because hope and fear are very good, we are told. But she went to a stage that said even hope and fear are something which would bar you from Allah himself. The story is told that once a number of Sufis saw her hurrying on her way with water in one hand. I said this before and a burning torch in the other when they asked her to explain she said, I want to throw fire in paradise and to pour water on to hell so that these 2 veils disappear and it becomes clear who worships God out of love and not out of fear of hell or hope of paradise which is well very interesting.

¶55 Now Michael Smith tells us that Rabia begun her ascetic life in a small desert cell near Basra, where she lost herself in prayer and went straight to God for teaching. As far as is known, she never studied under any masters or spiritual director. So she is different from those who had a silsilah of teachers and masters going back to the prophets. She was one of the first of the Sufis to teach that love alone was the guide on the mystical path. As her holiness became more widely known, numerous individuals beat her path to her doors, seeking her speech for direction. The path of Rabia and her mystical understanding which stood out very brilliantly was the path of zealous love for God.

¶56 She is generally regarded as the person who introduced the element of selfless love into the austere teaching of the earliest ascetic and gave mysticism the hue of true mysticism. This is true I mean the thesis and the heart of mysticism is love. It was missing before. I mean in other mystics, I'm not talking about teaching of immah. The other mystics love was missing. It was fear, it was asceticism. It was hardship. It was hereafter. Now here comes the heart of mysticism, the love of Allah. Now she has poetries and she has prayers. Now it is very difficult to choose from among many of her poetries and her prayers, those most beautiful ones, of course, in Arabic they are very beautiful.

¶57 But translating them into English it sometimes loses its sense. I have made thee the companion of my heart but my body is available for those who seek its company. Meaning I can live with the people but my heart is your companion and my body is friendly towards this guest. But the beloved of my heart is the guest of my soul, which is God of course. Another of her poetry is, I have 2 ways of loving you. This is a very famous poem of Rabia. I have 2 ways of loving you, a selfish one and another way that is worthy of you in my selfish love. I remember you and you alone. I say that because it is myself which wants it, deserves it.

¶58 I want to mention your name. I want to remember you. In that other love you live the veil. It's not me anymore. It's you who shows itself to me. It's not me who remembers you. It's you who comes to me. So a selfish love I'll come to you. In another love you come to me. And, O beloved of hearts, I have none like unto thee, therefore, have pity on the sinner, who comes to thee. All my hope and my rest and my delight, the heart can love none other but thee. And really cannot see when that place of God comes then we cannot love anything but thee. Now her prayers are very interesting as well.

¶59 Oh my Lord, if I worshipped thee from fear of hell, burn me in hell. And if I worship thee in hope of paradise, exclude me then. But if I worship thee for guide then behold not from me thy eternal beauty. If I worship you for hell, burn me for the fear of hell. It is for paradise do not give me paradise. But if I really worship you for yourself, then do not behold your beauty for me. Now another one, which is as well very beautiful. Oh God, whatever you have destined for me in this world, give it to your enemies. And whatever you have destined for me in the other world, give it to your friend since you are more than enough for me.

¶60 I don't want anything from you. This is very beautiful and it shows how actually she felt about hell and paradise and this is what Imam Ali (as) have said of course that some people worship God for fear of the hell. This is the worship of the slave and some people worship God for hope of paradise. And this is the worship of the businessman. But some people worship God because he deserves to be worshipped. And this is the worship of the free people who have free souls and free mind. And this is how of course this is realized in a lady like Rabia al Adawiya. As I said, many things about her and about many mystics are legends.

¶61 They are created later on due to respect that people had for them and it's difficult to distinguish between right and wrong. However, as their sayings, their poetries, their prayers are something which of course are not legends anymore. She was in her early to mid-80 when she died having followed the Mystic way to the end. By then she was continually united with her beloved as she told her Sufi friends, my beloved is always with me and of course, her collection just for the sake of those who are interested to read them, a collection of poems has been translated to English by Andrew Harvey and Eric Hunt in Perfume of the Deserts and by Charles Upton in Doorkeeper of the Hearts, versions of Rabia.

¶62 Well, those who are interested InshaAllah I will send you the slides. You could see them later. OK, let's go to our next mystic in overwhelming love, the know Al-Misri. He was a contemporary of Rabia, but much younger than Rabia. He transmitted tradition from Malik ibne Anas. Of course, he was a reporter as well. During the Mutazilites persecution of the Orthodox, he too was imprisoned for his belief in the belief that the Quran was uncreated; there are some extra words there. For his belief that the Quran was uncreated, he was accused of being a philosopher and an alchemist. Many miracles are ascribed to him, again, legend or reality we don't know but yes, he was a philosopher and especially since he was from Egypt and Egypt was at that time the cradle of these types of philosophical ideas.

¶63 It is quite probable that he had, as we see later he's told that he was influenced by Neo Platonic ideas which were prevalent in Egypt. He was representative of the School of Love in Mysticism, as I mentioned, and many things about love and intimacy are attributed to him. He used to say, oh, God, publicly I call thee, my Lord. This is very interesting as well. But in solitude, I call thee my beloved. In public you are Ya Rabb but in solitude you are my mahboob that I don't call you that. He formulated for the first time a theory of marifa intuitive knowledge as opposed to im, discursive knowledge. If you remember, at the beginning of the course, I distinguished between ilm and marifa.

¶64 Of course, this is not the way Quran uses. Quran uses ilm but mystics usually distinguish between a type of ilm which comes from within the heart, within the soul and the type of knowledge that comes from outside. And this is one of the innovations or one of the things which were introduced by Dhul-Nun al-Misri distinguishing between marifa and ilm. He is regarded by some to be the first philosophies among the Sufis. However, his poetic aspect is most conspicuous in his writings and even his poems are more developed than the poetry of Rabia which was very rudimentary. Nicholson believed that Dhul-Nun al-Misri was under the influence of Neo Platonism especially since he lived in Egypt, where those ideas were in the air and he also used to say that the sign of the lover of God is to follow the friend of God by the Prophet in his morals, his deeds and his orders and his customs.

¶65 So very orthodox of course despite of his mystical attitude. One said to the known, show me the greatest name of God. I told this because this is very beautiful. Show me the smallest. Say God has names and greatest names, but how do you actually judge between the greatest and the smallest? It is no small names and this is what many mystics say that all asmaullah or isme aazam are actually, but we do not realize it. And finally he composed charming poems and a new development in Sufism which of course was not there before him, although rather accredited with a few political exclamations. Mysticism of Gnosticism we leave it for next week Inshallah.

¶66 Wa sallahu ala mohammadin wa aale hittahereen.
